description: Subordinate Courts operate at the state level under the direct control and supervision of the High Court. Tribunals are quasi-judicial bodies established for the speedy and specialized disposal of specific types of disputes, introduced by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment.

sections.title: Subordinate Courts: Constitutional Provisions
sections.description: Part VI of the Constitution, from Articles 233 to 237, deals with the organization, functioning, and control of subordinate courts.

polity_articles.details: The appointment, posting, and promotion of district judges in a state are made by the Governor of the State in consultation with the High Court.
Appointments of persons other than district judges to the judicial service are made by the Governor in consultation with the State Public Service Commission and the High Court.
The administrative control over district courts and all other courts subordinate to them is completely vested in the High Court.

important_facts.fact: To be eligible for appointment as a District Judge, a person must have been an advocate or a pleader for a minimum of 7 years.

sections.title: Structure of District Courts
sections.description: The hierarchical structure of courts dealing with civil and criminal matters at the district level.

key_concepts.explanation: The highest judicial authority in a district. When presiding over civil cases, the judge is referred to as the 'District Judge'.
When the same District Judge presides over criminal cases, they are designated as the 'Sessions Judge'.
A criminal court subordinate to the Sessions Judge. The CJM has the authority to pass a sentence of imprisonment up to 7 years.

important_facts.fact: A Sessions Judge has the power to impose any legal sentence, including capital punishment (death sentence), but it must be confirmed by the High Court before execution.

sections.title: Lok Adalats and Gram Nyayalayas
sections.description: Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) mechanisms and grassroots-level justice delivery systems in India.

key_concepts.explanation: Based on Gandhian principles, Lok Adalats resolve pending cases or pre-litigation disputes through conciliation, mutual consent, and compromise.
Mobile courts established at the Panchayat level to ensure that justice reaches the doorsteps of citizens in rural areas.

historical_events.significance: This landmark act granted statutory status to Lok Adalats and formalized the legal aid mechanism in India.
Paved the way for the establishment of Gram Nyayalayas for speedy and easy access to justice system in the rural areas.

important_facts.fact: An award made by a Lok Adalat is deemed to be a decree of a civil court and is final and binding on all parties; no appeal lies against it in any court.

sections.title: Tribunals: Constitutional Framework
sections.description: Part XIV-A of the Constitution deals with Tribunals, created to reduce the burden on regular courts by handling specialized administrative and taxation disputes.

polity_articles.provision: Added a new Part XIV-A (Tribunals) to the Constitution.
polity_articles.details: This addition was primarily based on the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee.
Deals with disputes related to recruitment and conditions of service of public servants. These can be established only by the Parliament.
Deals with matters like taxation, foreign exchange, industrial and labour disputes, and land reforms. Both Parliament and State Legislatures can establish these.

key_associations.extra_info: It allows for only one tribunal at the center (CAT) and one for each state or two/more states (SAT). There is no hierarchy of tribunals under this article.
Unlike 323A, under this article, a hierarchy of tribunals can be created by the respective legislatures.

sections.title: Major National Tribunals
sections.description: Functions and historical origins of key central tribunals currently operating in India.

historical_events.significance: Led to the establishment of the Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) to adjudicate disputes and complaints regarding the service conditions of Union government employees.
Established the National Green Tribunal (NGT) for the effective and expeditious disposal of cases relating to environmental protection and conservation of forests.

important_facts.fact: In the landmark Chandra Kumar Case (1997), the Supreme Court ruled that the decisions of tribunals are subject to the writ jurisdiction of the High Courts, meaning appeals can be made against tribunal orders in the High Court.
The National Green Tribunal (NGT) is not bound by the strict procedural laws laid down under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, but is guided by the broader Principles of Natural Justice.
